“By eight o’clock I had actually risen seventeen miles above the earth. It therefore seemed clear that my speed was increasing and that some acceleration would have been noticeable even without the ballast I had thrown out. The pain in my head and ears returned in violent bursts, and my nose still bled occasionally. Overall, though, I suffered much less than one might have expected. Breathing, on the other hand, grew harder every moment, and each inhalation brought an uncomfortable spasm in my chest. I unpacked the equipment for condensing air and prepared it for immediate use.

“At this stage of the ascent, the earth looked truly beautiful. To the west, north, and south, as far as I could see, stretched an endless sheet of apparently calm ocean. Its blue deepened moment by moment, and its surface was already beginning to look slightly curved. Far to the east, yet clearly visible, lay the islands of Great Britain, the entire Atlantic coastlines of France and Spain, and a small part of northern Africa. No individual building could be made out. Humanity’s proudest cities had vanished completely from the face of the earth. From Gibraltar, now reduced to a faint speck, the dark Mediterranean extended eastward to the limit of my sight, its bright islands scattered like stars across the sky. Eventually its whole expanse seemed to plunge over the abyss at the horizon, and I found myself standing on tiptoe, listening for echoes of that enormous waterfall. Above me, the sky was jet black and the stars shone brilliantly.

“The pigeons now appeared to be suffering badly, so I decided to release them. First I untied a beautiful bird mottled with gray and set him on the edge of the wicker basket. He seemed extremely distressed, looking anxiously around, fluttering his wings, and cooing loudly, but nothing could persuade him to leave the basket. Finally, I picked him up and tossed him about six yards away from the balloon. Instead of descending as I expected, he struggled fiercely to return, uttering shrill, piercing cries. At last he regained his former perch on the rim. Almost immediately, however, his head fell against his breast, and he dropped dead into the basket.

“Each compares it to a speaker of a language he does not know, rather than one he understands. The Frenchman thinks the voice was Spanish and says he ‘might have picked out words if he knew Spanish.’ The Dutchman insists it was French, but the report tells us that ‘the witness does not understand French and was questioned through an interpreter.’ The Englishman believes it was German, though he ‘does not understand German.’ The Spaniard is ‘certain’ it was an Englishman, but bases this entirely on the sound, ‘since he knows no English.’ The Italian thinks it was a Russian, yet ‘has never spoken with anyone from Russia.’ A second Frenchman disagrees with the first and is sure the speaker was Italian; but he too does not know that language and, like the Spaniard, relies on intonation. Consider how extraordinarily unfamiliar that voice must have been to produce testimony like this! Even its tones sounded recognizable to none of these people from Europe’s five great divisions. You may suggest it belonged to someone from Asia or Africa. Neither Asians nor Africans are numerous in Paris, but without rejecting your suggestion, let me draw attention to three points. One witness describes the voice as ‘harsh rather than high-pitched.’ Two others call it ‘rapid and irregular.’ Not one witness reports distinguishing any words, or even sounds that resembled words.

“I do not know,” Dupin continued, “what impression these observations have made on you so far. But I can confidently say that sound deductions from this testimony alone—the evidence about the gruff and high-pitched voices—are enough to raise a suspicion that should guide every further step of the investigation. ‘Sound deductions’ does not quite convey my meaning. I mean they are the only correct conclusions, and that this suspicion follows inevitably from them as the sole possible result. I will not yet tell you what that suspicion is. For now, simply remember that it was strong enough to give my examination of the room a definite shape and direction.

“Let us imagine ourselves back in that room. What should we look for first? The route by which the murderers escaped. I think I can safely say that neither of us believes in supernatural events.

Mr. Merton was considerably troubled by the marriage being postponed a second time. Lady Julia, whose wedding dress had already been ordered, exerted herself in every way to persuade Sybil to abandon the engagement. Yet, fondly as Sybil loved her mother, she had placed her entire life in Lord Arthur’s keeping, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake that trust. Lord Arthur, meanwhile, required several days to recover from his dreadful disappointment, and for a while his nerves were utterly disordered. Soon, however, his admirable common sense prevailed, and his sensible, practical intelligence left him in little doubt about his next step. Since poison had failed entirely, dynamite, or another kind of explosive, was plainly the appropriate thing to attempt.

He therefore reviewed his list of relations and friends and, after due reflection, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. A gentleman of considerable cultivation and scholarship, the Dean was passionately interested in clocks. His remarkable collection of timepieces extended from the fifteenth century to the present, and this innocent enthusiasm seemed to Lord Arthur to provide an excellent means of executing his plan. Obtaining an explosive device was naturally a different problem. The London Directory supplied no guidance, and he doubted that approaching Scotland Yard would be useful. They appeared to learn nothing of the dynamite faction’s activities until an explosion had occurred, and even then learned very little.

Then he suddenly remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with pronounced revolutionary inclinations, whom he had encountered at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be preparing a biography of Peter the Great and to have travelled to England to examine documents concerning the Tsar’s residence there as a ship carpenter. General opinion, however, suspected him of being a Nihilist agent, and the Russian Embassy unquestionably regarded his presence in London with disapproval. Lord Arthur believed him precisely the person he needed. One morning he drove to the Count’s Bloomsbury lodgings to request advice and help.

‘So you are becoming seriously involved in politics?’ Count Rouvaloff asked, after Lord Arthur had explained his errand. But Lord Arthur, who abhorred every kind of swagger, felt obliged to confess that social questions did not interest him in the slightest. He wanted the explosive device only for a strictly domestic affair, which concerned nobody except himself.
